Listen to this article Share Bayo Adalemo is a Nigerian architect, entrepreneur and educator whose work spans architecture, real estate development, hospitality and higher education. With a career rooted in design, business leadership and the built environment, he brings together a multidisciplinary perspective on how spaces are designed, businesses are built and people are empowered to realise their potential. He is the Managing Director of Design Protocol, a Lagos-based real estate development and construction company focused on delivering thoughtfully designed, functional and sustainable spaces. Under his leadership, the company has undertaken residential development projects, including Admiralty Pearl, a residential development on Admiralty Road, Lekki Phase 1, Lagos. His approach to the built environment reflects an appreciation for the relationship between design, functionality, quality of life and longterm value. Beyond architecture and real estate, Adalemo has interests in hospitality and experiential living through Zen Cafe, extending his entrepreneurial footprint into the food, beverage and lifestyle sector. His ventures reflect a broader interest in how the spaces people inhabit, the services they experience and the environments they interact with shape everyday life. Adalemo also serves in academia at the University of Lagos, contributing to the development of future professionals through teaching and knowledge sharing. His connection to the institution is personal as well as professional: he studied Architecture there, having developed an early interest in drawing and fine art. In an interview with BDWeekender, Adalemo speaks on balancing aesthetic design with commercial viability in Lagos, navigating the complexities of gentrification in high-density areas, and why sustainable architecture in Nigeria is a survival strategy rather than a luxury. He also discusses his transition into lifestyle hospitality with Zen Cafe, bridging the gap between classroom theory and real-world real estate site execution, and how homegrown materials and technology can redefine the future of Nigeria’s built environment. As an architect leading a real estate development firm like Design Protocol, how do you balance aesthetic design with commercial viability in a market like Lagos? Many of our projects are partnerships with landowners, and their aim is clear: to realize the full commercial value of their property and make the most of every square meter the site and the planning regulations allow. In real estate terms, they want the land’s “highest and best use.” So the commercials are key; they are the reason the project exists. Our job is to balance that with aesthetic appeal. A plot packed to its limit with little thought and consideration for its occupants may look good on a spreadsheet, but it won’t sell, let or hold its value. We put design effort into what people experience every day: light, ventilation, circulation and the arrival experience. We are ruthless about cost where it adds nothing. Every design decision has a return-on-capital question attached to it. That balance is a big part of why Design Protocol grew its annual revenue tenfold in under five years without sacrificing the quality our name stands for. Projects like Admiralty Pearl on Admiralty Road sit in high-density, rapidly evolving areas. What unique architectural and structural challenges did you navigate during its development? First, a quick update: the project formerly known as Admiralty Pearl is now Pleasant View Estate. Admiralty Road is a good example of Lekki’s growing pains. It is being gentrified at an alarming rate, which is a subject close to my heart, as it forms the thrust of my PhD thesis at UNILAG on the impact of gentrification in emerging cities. So I am very conscious that a development is not just a building; it changes the character of a neighborhood and who can afford to live in it. Land is expensive, plots are tight, traffic is heavy, and the area changes almost month to month. The first challenge was fitting 20 units on a constrained plot while still giving each home the easements that guarantee a great standard of living. The second was the soil. Much of Lekki is reclaimed or high-water-table land, so foundations and drainage need serious engineering attention from day one. We used pile foundations, driving the load down past the loose upper soil to firmer ground, so the building stays stable for decades on difficult terrain. Then there was logistics: moving materials and labor in and out along a busy road without disrupting neighbors. Finally, we designed for where the area is going, not where it is today, with garage parking, home offices, solar water heaters, our own sewage treatment plant, jetties for waterfront access, and a large green area for recreation. The estate has been future-proofed against density that has not yet arrived. What does “sustainable and functional living” mean in the context of Nigerian real estate, where infrastructure deficits often challenge long-term building maintenance? In Nigeria, sustainability can’t be a luxury add-on; it’s a survival strategy. If public power, water and drainage are unreliable, the building itself has to do more of the work. To me, that starts with passive design: orientation, cross-ventilation, shading and natural light, which cut energy demand before you spend a kobo on equipment. Then comes resilience: solar and backup power, water harvesting and treatment, and drainage designed for our rainfall. Just as important is maintainability. A building is only sustainable if it can be cared for over the decades with locally available skills and materials. This forms a large part of my research focus. My MSc in Sustainable Development from the University of Sussex and my research at UNILAG are both about making green building practical for our context, rather than imported theory. What inspired your transition into the food, beverage, and lifestyle sector with Zen Cafe, and how does your background in spatial architecture influence the guest experience there? Honestly, it’s less a transition than a homecoming. As a student at UNILAG decades ago, I ran a restaurant called QSS, and we pioneered the sale of chicken and chips within the university community. That was my baptism, so to speak, into entrepreneurship, and it taught me early lessons about people, process, quality and cash flow that I still use. So when the opportunity came to open Zen Cafe, it felt like a natural progression. Architecture has always been about how people feel in a space, and a cafe is the most immediate test of that. You know within a minute whether a guest feels at ease or not. At Zen Cafe, on Adebayo Doherty Road in Lekki Phase 1, the space does a lot of the hosting. We thought carefully about the flow from the entrance to the counter and on to your seat, the balance of light and shade, acoustics, and giving people both sociable and quiet corners. Greenery is central to the experience. There are plants and green spaces in and around the cafe, so guests feel surrounded by nature the moment they arrive. As the name implies, Zen Cafe is meant to be an oasis. In a city as intense as Lagos, people want a place where they can exhale. Designing that calm is an architectural problem as much as a culinary one. How do you see the relationship between real estate, hospitality, and overall quality of life evolving for young professionals and families in urban centers? The lines between them are disappearing. Young professionals in Lagos increasingly judge a home by what is within ten minutes of it: somewhere to work, eat, exercise and meet people. Long commutes have made the neighborhood part of the product. So developers can no longer just sell four walls; we have to think about the whole street and its urban context. I expect more mixed-use developments, more shared amenities and more hospitality-style services inside residential buildings. For families, it’s about safety, green space and good schools nearby. The developers who succeed will be those who design for how people actually live, not just for floor area. Your late father, Emeritus Professor Isaac Adalemo, and your mentor, Professor David Aradeon, played pivotal roles in your journey. How did their influence shape your perspective as both an architect and an educator at UNILAG? I literally grew up on the UNILAG campus, so the university has never been just a workplace to me; it’s home. My father taught me that knowledge only matters when it serves people. He was a respected scholar who also served as a visiting professor at several universities in the U.S. and as a consultant to both the World Bank and the United Nations. He moved fluidly between the lecture hall and real-world policy, and I saw early that the two should feed each other. The late Professor Aradeon, on the other hand, polished my architectural lens. He was a master of pedagogy who believed in one-on-one interaction with his students, and he always encouraged and supported me. I try to teach the same way. Between them, I learned that an architect has a responsibility to society, not just to a client. That’s why, alongside running Design Protocol, I teach as a Lecturer II in the Department of Architecture while also pursuing my PhD there. Through Design Protocol’s EmpowerMD CSR initiative, children get to experience being “Managing Director for a Day.” What has been the most fulfilling feedback or outcome you’ve seen from these young minds? The most fulfilling thing is watching a child’s sense of what is possible expand, and then seeing it last. Chimamanda Isiakpona was our very first child MD for a day. At the second edition of the event a year later, I was moderating the fireside chat, and she took over the entire conversation. She wowed the audience with her knowledge of leadership, sustainability and the environment, and she credited part of it to the confidence she had gained since becoming child MD the year before. For me, that moment said everything. Children ask the questions adults stop asking: “Why is it done this way?” “Why can’t we do it better?” That is exactly the mindset I try to build in my own teams. The aim isn’t to create future MDs overnight. It’s to show children that leadership is something you practice, not something reserved for other people. What is the biggest knowledge gap you see in today’s architecture students when transitioning from the UNILAG classroom to the real estate site? The biggest gap is the business side of architecture: entrepreneurial training. Our students graduate with strong design skills, but many have never seen a budget, a cash-flow forecast or a contract document. On site, they discover that every line they draw has a cost, a sequence and a person who has to build it. Those realities can make or break a project. The second gap is buildability and materiology: understanding how things are actually put together, and what’s available locally. I’m in an unusual position, teaching in the morning and running a development company the rest of the day, so I try to bring the site into the classroom. I’d love to see more structured internships and more practitioners teaching alongside academics. At the Blueprint Conference, you emphasized the need for closer collaboration between property developers and interior designers. Why do you feel this disconnect still exists in the local industry? Mostly because of sequence and habit. In many Nigerian projects, the interior designer is brought in after the structure is finished, almost as a decorator. By then the ceiling heights, window positions, service runs and power points are fixed. The designer spends the budget working around decisions that could have been made better at the start. Developers sometimes see interiors as a cost to minimize rather than as the value that sells the property. I’ve been on both sides of this; I’m an architect, and I’ve served as Assistant Secretary General of the Interior Designers Association of Nigeria. The fix is simple: bring interior designers to the table at the concept stage. You get better spaces, fewer costly changes, and a product that sells faster. With rising import costs and currency shifts, how can Nigeria’s built environment sector lean more into local talent, homegrown materials, and indigenous solutions without compromising luxury or structural standards? The currency crisis is painful, but it’s also forcing a conversation we should have had decades ago. Luxury is not the same as imported. Some of the most beautiful buildings in the world use local stone, timber, clay and craft brilliantly. Nigeria has good materials, from laterite and stabilized earth blocks to local stone and timber, and a huge pool of artisans. What we lack is standardization, testing and certification, so developers can trust local products at scale. That’s where industry, regulators and universities must work together. The encouraging news is that the demand is already there. As pioneer Chairman of the Board of CutStruct, a construction-technology company, I helped launch a B2B procurement platform that now has thousands of users across Nigeria and partners with homegrown manufacturers such as Dangote, African Foundries and Quantum Steel. What we see on that platform is clear: when local products are well made and reliably supplied, developers buy them. So leaning local doesn’t mean lowering standards. It means investing in quality control so that homegrown becomes a premium choice, not a compromise. How are emerging technologies (such as digital modeling, smart home tech, or sustainable building materials) reshaping how Design Protocol plans its future developments? Technology is changing how we plan, build and sell. Digital modeling and BIM let us catch clashes and cost overruns on screen instead of on site, which in this economy is worth a lot. Smart home features, such as energy monitoring, security and access control, are becoming expected, especially by younger buyers, who tend to be more discerning. On the sustainability side, we’re looking closely at solar integration, energy-efficient envelopes and alternative materials. Digital procurement is also bringing much-needed transparency and efficiency to building supply chains. Our rule is simple: we adopt technology that solves a real problem for the occupant or the project, not technology for its own sake. Looking across your roles as an architect, developer, restaurateur, educator, and mentor, which identity feels closest to your core vision? If I had to choose one, I’d say builder, in the widest sense. I build spaces as an architect and developer, experiences as a restaurateur, and people as a teacher and mentor. But if you pushed me, the educator sits closest to my heart. I am my father’s son, and I grew up watching what a teacher can do for a nation. Buildings last decades; the people you train shape a country for generations. Everything else I do, from running Design Protocol to Zen Cafe, gives me real experience to bring back to the classroom. The roles feed each other, and I’ve stopped seeing them as separate. What is the next major chapter or horizon for Design Protocol in shaping Nigeria’s urban landscape? The next chapter is about scale and responsibility. Nigeria’s cities are growing faster than our housing and infrastructure can keep up with. We want Design Protocol to show that you can build well-designed, sustainable and financially sound developments at a larger scale. Concretely, that means putting more emphasis on green building, mixed-use communities and local materials, and continuing to invest in young talent, because the industry needs a new generation of builders. My long-term ambition is for Design Protocol to be known not just for what we built, but for how we raised the standard of building in Nigeria.
